stimulus.text:
“His Britannic Majesty acknowledges the said United States, viz., New Hampshire, Massachusetts Bay, Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia, to be free sovereign and independent states, that he treats with them as such, and for himself, his heirs, and successors, relinquishes all claims to the government, propriety, and territorial rights of the same and every part thereof.”
—Treaty of Paris, Article 1, September 3, 1783 (abridged)
stimulus.source_note: Treaty of Paris, September 3, 1783. Public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

stem: In the Treaty of Paris, the United States promised in return that

options.text: Britain could keep troops in forts on American soil
options.misconception: Britain did keep troops in western forts after the war, but that was a British refusal to leave, not a promise in the treaty.

options.text: The United States would rejoin the British Empire as a dominion
options.misconception: The treaty recognizes the United States as free, sovereign, and independent states; rejoining the empire is the opposite of what it does.

options.text: American merchants would trade only with Britain
options.misconception: The treaty sets no such limit; American merchants were free to trade with other nations, including France.

options.text: Loyalists could seek their confiscated property and prewar debts would be paid

rationales.D: The treaty provided that Loyalists could seek their confiscated property through the courts and that prewar debts to British merchants would be paid.
rationales.A: British troops stayed in the western forts, but that was Britain holding on, not a term the United States promised.
rationales.B: The treaty recognizes independence; rejoining the empire would undo the very thing it establishes.
rationales.C: No trade limit was set; the United States traded with France and others after the war.
rationales.general:
1. Read what America gives. Recognition and land came from Britain, so ask what Britain got back.
2. Find the promises. Loyalists could go to court for confiscated property, and prewar debts to British merchants were to be paid.
3. Rule out the rest. No troops, no reunion, and no trade limit appear in the treaty.
Remember: a peace has two sides — after the headline concession, ask what the winner promised in return.
